title: India to Launch Unified Customer ID for Banks and Insurers in August
excerpt: The CKYC 2.0 system will let financial institutions pull verified customer data from a central registry with consent, eliminating repeated KYC paperwork. Mutual funds and brokerages are expected to join later this year.
body:
• Indian banks and insurance companies will roll out a common customer identification system called CKYC 2.0 in August, according to Reuters, citing regulatory sources and industry executives.
  • The system draws on a central registry of roughly 1.2 billion records, adding confidence scores so institutions can gauge data reliability before onboarding customers.
  • Mutual funds, brokerages, and other capital markets firms are expected to join within four months as regulators finalise sector-specific requirements.
  • For the Indian diaspora managing accounts across banks, insurers, and investment platforms, the change could mean simpler remote onboarding and fewer document submissions.

Indian banks and insurers will begin using a unified customer identification system in August, two regulatory sources and industry executives told Reuters, a move designed to let customers open accounts and buy financial products without submitting the same documents to each institution separately.

The upgraded system, Central Know-Your-Customer 2.0 (CKYC), requires only a customer's one-time password consent for a financial institution to pull verified identity data from a central registry. The Reserve Bank of India, the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), and the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) are jointly executing the project, though none responded to Reuters' requests for comment.

Why the Overhaul Was Needed

India already maintains a central KYC registry containing approximately 1.2 billion customer records, but the database has been underused. Data quality concerns—duplicate entries, missing fields—led the RBI to refuse records sourced from it, forcing customers to file fresh documents every time they opened a bank account, bought insurance, or started a mutual fund.

The country has spent more than a decade trying to build a system comparable to Singapore's and several European nations' digital identity frameworks, where a single verified identity unlocks access to multiple financial products.

"The accuracy score wouldn't just provide consented data, but through this matrix it will also tell them how much to trust it."

— Rakesh Dosi, Chief Business and Product Officer, Protean eGov Technologies

Under the new design, each record will carry a confidence score indicating how accurate and recently verified the data is—and which institution verified it. Financial firms will then request access via a customer's OTP, according to operating guidelines reviewed by Reuters.

Scope and Rollout Timeline

Banks and insurance companies go first. Paras Pasricha, business head at Policybazaar, India's largest insurance marketplace, told Reuters that insurers are building the necessary capabilities and expect a phase to go live by August.

Capital markets participants—mutual funds, brokerages, and other intermediaries—are expected to follow later this year as regulators sort out sector-specific requirements. DP Singh, joint chief executive of SBI Funds Management, India's largest asset manager, said the framework could be operational for the mutual fund industry within four months.

"Even if a fraction of eligible customers begin investing after universal customer identification, the upside will be significant."

— DP Singh, Joint CEO, SBI Funds Management

Singh pointed to the scale of the opportunity: State Bank of India, SBI Funds' largest shareholder and the country's biggest bank by assets, holds 500 million bank accounts. Universal identification could convert a slice of those depositors into mutual fund investors.

Technical Architecture

CKYC 2.0 replaces the old batch-processed, largely static database with a real-time, API-driven platform, according to SEBI's earlier disclosures. The system is expected to integrate with Aadhaar, UPI, the Account Aggregator framework, and DigiLocker, enabling instant verification and synchronised updates across participating entities.

AI-assisted deduplication is a core feature: the platform will identify and merge duplicate KYC records maintained across institutions, addressing a longstanding pain point in the existing registry. An event-driven architecture means any change in customer information can be reflected across connected systems in near real-time, reducing fragmentation.

The technology is being built by Protean eGov Technologies, while the Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India (CERSAI) maintains the registry itself. SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey has called authentication the system's biggest challenge, warning that weak initial verification could make the shared data pool "untrustworthy."

The Bigger Picture

The push reflects India's strategic shift from basic financial inclusion to deeper product penetration. About 89% of Indian adults owned bank accounts in 2024, according to World Bank data, but participation in mutual funds, insurance, and pensions remains comparatively low. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman underlined the urgency at SEBI's 38th Foundation Day in April, calling for a "seamless, secure and portable" KYC experience that lets citizens move between financial services without repeating verification steps.

For NRIs and the broader diaspora, CKYC 2.0 could reduce friction when managing Indian financial accounts remotely—a process that currently requires separate KYC submissions to each institution, often with physical document attestation. A consent-based, digitally verified system could simplify cross-border account management and make it easier to invest in Indian markets from abroad.

What to Watch

Execution risk remains. The system's success hinges on whether financial institutions can upgrade their technology stacks quickly enough, how robust the consent and authentication layers prove to be, and whether the confidence-scoring mechanism gains trust across the industry. If it works, India will have built one of the largest unified financial identity systems in the world—a prerequisite for the next phase of its fintech ambitions.
